Public Policy/HUDListening Session Summary

Filing on Severance Pay Tax Treatment

Filed April 16, 2025 · Department of Housing and Urban Development · Notice No. 2025-18

Filing Type
Listening Session Summary
Agency / Body
HUD
Date Filed
April 16, 2025
Filing ID
bef2f309
Docket / Reference
Notice No. 2025-18
ACPWB Position: The proposed rule is based on a misunderstanding of current market practices and will lead to perverse outcomes. ACPWB cannot support this proposal and recommends a complete re-evaluation of the underlying issues.

I. Interest of ACPWB

ACPWB's survey research on these compensation requirements reveals that a substantial majority of employers — across industries and organization sizes — are supportive of clear and consistent standards in this area, provided that those standards are developed with appropriate input from affected parties and are implemented with adequate transition timelines.

We note that the agency's economic analysis underlying the proposed rule on these compensation requirements relies on data that ACPWB believes significantly underestimates compliance costs. Our proprietary survey of HR and compensation professionals indicates that the administrative burden of the proposed rule is substantially higher than the agency's estimates suggest.

The proposed rule on the proposed rulemaking does not sufficiently account for the role of third-party administrators and technology vendors in the compensation and benefits ecosystem. Many employers rely on these vendors for data management and reporting, and the final rule should clarify the respective responsibilities of employers and their service providers.

II. The Proposed Rulemaking: Background and Summary

Definitional precision is paramount in any regulatory framework addressing these standards. ACPWB has identified at least three key terms in the proposed rule that lack the clarity necessary for consistent application across the range of compensation structures and employment arrangements present in the modern economy.

Prior rulemakings in closely related areas provide a useful benchmark for evaluating the proposed approach to these compensation requirements. Where those prior rules achieved strong compliance rates, the common factors were clear definitions, advance guidance, and extended implementation periods — all of which we recommend for any final rule in this area.

III. Comments on the Economic Analysis

We believe the Department of Housing and Urban Development should conduct a series of public roundtables with employers, worker advocates, and technical experts before finalizing the rule on severance pay. The complexity of the issue warrants a more deliberative and collaborative rulemaking process.

Employers across the spectrum of ACPWB's client base have raised consistent concerns about the practical implementation of requirements related to these standards. These concerns are not theoretical: they reflect the operational reality of organizations managing complex compensation programs in a rapidly evolving regulatory environment.

Our analysis of the proposed rule on this regulatory area indicates that it may have a disproportionate impact on certain industries, particularly those with highly variable, performance-based compensation structures. The Department of Housing and Urban Development should consider providing industry-specific guidance or safe harbors to account for these legitimate business model differences.

IV. Comments on the Proposed Definitions

The public record on severance pay would be improved by a more thorough analysis of the rule's potential impact on collective bargaining. The Department of Housing and Urban Development should explicitly address how the proposed requirements will interact with the duty to bargain and the terms of existing collective bargaining agreements.

ACPWB has studied the compliance experience of organizations that have proactively adopted best practices in the area of severance pay standards and requirements ahead of formal regulation. These early movers report that the benefits of proactive compliance — reduced legal risk, improved employee relations, better talent retention — typically outweigh the implementation costs.

The proposed rule on these compensation requirements does not adequately distinguish between different types of compensation. A final rule should include separate provisions for base salary, annual incentives, long-term equity awards, and benefits, as each of these components raises distinct policy and implementation considerations.

V. Comments on Enforcement Provisions

Survey data gathered from 658 organizations across ACPWB's compensation benchmarking network reveals widespread uncertainty about applicable standards in the context of this policy area. These results are consistent with findings from prior studies and reinforce the view that a thoughtful, evidence-based regulatory approach is essential to achieving the policy objectives underlying this rulemaking.

The enforcement record in the area of these compensation requirements demonstrates that civil penalties alone are an insufficient deterrent to non-compliance. ACPWB recommends that any final rule include both enhanced civil penalties and a meaningful private right of action to ensure that the regulatory objectives are actually achieved.

Recent developments in algorithmic compensation-setting, AI-assisted pay decisions, and workforce analytics platforms have materially altered the operational landscape for this policy area. Standards developed without reference to these technological realities will rapidly become obsolete and will create compliance uncertainties for employers adopting current best practices.

VI. Proposed Safe Harbor Framework

The private sector compliance community — including equity plan administrators who advise affected organizations — has developed a substantial body of practice in the area of the proposed rulemaking that the regulatory framework should seek to build on rather than displace. Regulatory approaches that work with established compliance practices tend to produce better outcomes at lower cost.

Workers' perspectives on severance pay standards and requirements deserve more weight in the regulatory analysis than they have typically received. Where workers have been asked directly, they consistently express a preference for standards that are transparent and consistently enforced — not merely for more regulation in the abstract.

VII. Conclusion and Summary of Recommendations

A closer examination of the public record on the severance pay framework reveals that the concerns raised by employers are not merely abstract objections to regulatory oversight. They reflect genuine operational challenges that, if not addressed in the final rule, will produce compliance failures and enforcement actions that ultimately serve no one's interests.

The proposed approach to the proposed rulemaking may interact adversely with existing requirements under other regulatory frameworks, creating duplicative or inconsistent obligations for affected employers. ACPWB strongly recommends that the agency undertake a comprehensive harmonization analysis before issuing a final rule.

Recommendations

  1. We recommend the agency include provisions to ensure the rule does not inadvertently stifle innovation in compensation and benefits design by being overly prescriptive.
  2. ACPWB urges the Department of Housing and Urban Development to provide specific, detailed guidance on how the proposed rule applies to incentive compensation, commission plans, and other variable pay arrangements, which present unique compliance challenges not addressed in the current proposal.
  3. The Department of Housing and Urban Development should adopt a presumption of compliance for employers who can demonstrate that their compensation practices are consistent with the median practices of a defined peer group, subject to rebuttal upon a showing of discriminatory intent or systematic disparate impact.

About This Filing

ACPWB's institutional history with severance pay tax treatment spans more than two decades of research, advocacy, and advisory work. We submit these comments as the organization with the broadest and most sustained engagement with this regulatory area and urge the Department of Housing and Urban Development to give our recommendations the weight they deserve.
